title: The beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 1:7; 3:5–6)
hookLine: trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding

cards: Three words most adults find surprisingly hard to say: I don't know. We'll guess, bluff, change the subject, or look it up under the table first. Not knowing feels like weakness.
Yet almost everyone has met the opposite kind of person, a doctor, a grandmother, a mechanic, who says I don't know easily and somehow becomes more trustworthy for it.
Today, the book of Proverbs, a collection of sayings about how to live well. Its first big idea isn't about being clever. It's about where wisdom starts.

teach.b: Proverbs opens with a heading: "The proverbs of Solomon the son of David, king of Israel."
But inside, other collections carry other names: sayings copied by the men of King Hezekiah, the words of Agur, the words of King Lemuel. It's a library gathered over generations.
Then the motto for the whole book, in the King James Bible: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction."
You heard nearly the same line at the end of Job's poem on wisdom.

The Hebrew for beginning is reshit, the same word hidden in the Bible's first line, in the beginning. It can mean the starting point, and also the first and best part. Awe of God isn't the finish line of wisdom.
It's the first step, and the foundation. Now today's word. Wisdom in Hebrew is chokhmah, and it's surprisingly practical.
The same word describes the craftsmen who built the tabernacle in Exodus, filled with wisdom to work in gold and wood and cloth.
Wisdom is know-how: skill at living. And in Proverbs, wisdom is pictured as a woman who stands in the street and calls out to anyone passing.
Then chapter three: "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths."
Lean not doesn't mean stop thinking; Proverbs is full of hard thinking.

teach.h: DON'T PUT YOUR WHOLE WEIGHT ON IT
teach.b: It means don't put your whole weight on it, like a walking stick that might snap.

teach.h: TRUST IN THE LORD WITH ALL THINE HEART.
teach.b: And directing paths, in Hebrew, means making them straight.

how: Many Christians memorize Proverbs 3:5–6 and pray it before decisions, and some read one chapter of Proverbs a day, one for each day of the month.

games.q: you're compiling a book of wisdom for young people. what do you put first, as the motto?
o: the fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge.
games.why: Proverbs 1:7. awe of God is the first step and foundation, before any of the practical advice.

practice: Think of a question you've been pretending to have answered: how a relationship will turn out, whether a decision was right, something about God. Name it plainly, I don't know, and let that be okay for a little while.
If you pray, say the line, trust in the Lord with all thine heart; if not, rest your weight on something other than having the answer.

wordCard.voice: Wisdom. In Hebrew, chokhmah: skill at living, the know-how of a craftsman, which Proverbs says begins in awe of God.
